summary: Defines a canonical text format for writing IPv6 addresses, because the flexible forms allowed by RFC 4291 caused problems for operators and users. Implementations should write this form but still accept any legal form. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5952 gives people and systems one consistent way to write an IPv6 address. This makes addresses easier to find and compare, while older valid spellings still have to be accepted.

questions: how to write an ipv6 address
what is the canonical ipv6 text format
subtitle: A consistent way to write IPv6 addresses so people and tools can compare them reliably.

tldr.problem: RFC 4291 permits several spellings for one IPv6 address. Those differences make searching, comparing and checking addresses harder.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends one written form: remove leading zeros, shorten the longest run of zero fields, choose the first run when tied, and use lowercase letters.
tldr.outcome: Systems should generate the recommended form, but must still accept every valid RFC 4291 form. This document updates RFC 4291.

facts.label: Compression tie rule
facts.value: Shorten the first equally long zero run

today: RFC 5952 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4291. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 5952.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Needs a Standard Spelling
sections.content:
One IPv6 address can have many text spellings. RFC 4291 allows variation in leading zeros, zero compression, and letter case, so two strings can represent the same address.

This flexibility creates problems when people search records or compare configuration files. RFC 5952 chooses a recommended text form, but does not define how software stores addresses internally.
sections.plainLanguage: One IPv6 address can be written in several valid ways. A shared spelling makes it easier to recognize the same address in logs, lists, and settings.

sections.title: The Choices in RFC 4291
sections.content:
A 16-bit field may include or omit leading zeros. The double colon (::) can stand for one or more zero fields, and RFC 4291 does not prefer uppercase or lowercase hexadecimal letters.

Because :: can appear only once, an address with multiple zero runs may have more than one compressed spelling. These choices explain why a single address can look different in separate systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier rules allowed writers to choose whether to show extra zeros, where to shorten zeros, and which letter case to use. Each choice could produce a different-looking address.

sections.title: Problems Caused by Different Spellings
sections.content:
Exact text searches can miss an address written in another valid form. That can mislead address checks, network troubleshooting, and searches through records or diagrams.

Different spellings can also create noisy configuration comparisons and confusion when a system displays an address differently from the operator's input. Text comparison can be unsafe for access control; the RFC notes that X.509 address comparisons are commonly done in binary form.
sections.plainLanguage: A text search may miss an address when another system uses a different valid spelling. For access decisions, software should compare the address value rather than its written characters.

sections.title: Rules for the Recommended Form
sections.content:
Systems SHOULD use this form when writing IPv6 addresses, and all implementations MUST accept any legitimate RFC 4291 form. Leading zeros in a field MUST be removed; a field containing only zeros is written as 0.

Use :: for the longest run of zero fields, but not for a single zero field. If two runs tie, shorten the first. Letters from a through f MUST be lowercase.
sections.plainLanguage: Remove extra zeros, use two colons for the longest useful run of zeros, and write letters in lowercase. If two zero runs are equally long, shorten the first one.

sections.title: Special Addresses, Ports and Prefixes
sections.content:
Some IPv6 addresses contain an IPv4 address in their final 32 bits. For these addresses, mixed hexadecimal and dotted-decimal notation is RECOMMENDED when a well-known prefix identifies the embedded IPv4 address. The hexadecimal portion still follows the normal rules.

When adding a port number, the bracket form from RFC 3986, such as [2001:db8::1]:80, SHOULD be used. The form without brackets is ambiguous. IPv6 prefixes should follow the same text rules as addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Some addresses can show their final IPv4 part with dots. Put an IPv6 address in square brackets before adding a port, so the port is easy to tell apart.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Comparing IPv6 addresses as text can create a security risk when the result controls access. Different spellings of the same address may be treated as different values by a simple text comparison.

The RFC says X.509 address data is commonly compared in binary form. That avoids relying on how the address was written.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not use a simple text comparison to decide whether two IPv6 addresses are equal. Compare their address values instead.
